proof:
# A uniform ordinary Lorentz neighborhood among quadrilaterals

This proves a neighborhood theorem for bodies with at most four vertices, not for arbitrary convex bodies. Its endpoint argument handles concentrating ears by exact geometry; it does not infer a uniform neighborhood from pointwise negative first derivatives.

## 1. Statement and proved inputs

Fix an interior source y and three spanning balanced normals v1+v2+v3=0. For a convex planar body K containing y in its interior define

    k=|K|, Qi=|K intersect {vi.(x-y)>=0}|,
    sigma_i=H1(K intersect {vi.(x-y)=0})/||vi||,
    M=sum_i Qi/sigma_i,
    Fi=2 sqrt(k Qi)/(sigma_i M),
    Phi_i=Fi+(Fj+Fk)^2/4.

Let T0 be a triangle whose three source cuts strictly isolate distinct vertices. Fix a row i with Phi_i(T0)=2.

**Theorem.** There is a Hausdorff neighborhood of T0 such that every triangle or quadrilateral K in that neighborhood satisfies Phi_i(K)<=2. Every genuine quadrilateral there satisfies the strict inequality. The source remains interior throughout a sufficiently small such neighborhood. Intersecting the finitely many row neighborhoods and using continuity for initially strict rows gives all three Lorentz inequalities, strict for every genuine quadrilateral.

The inputs are the proved actual-triangle Lorentz theorem; the strict double-sector ear derivatives from `candidate cfb017a0e12acfbf` and `candidate 146226205b30285c`; the strict unique-sector derivatives in `candidate 8e1d01c76d1a2560`; and the strict corner-removal derivative in `candidate bb526889825517af`. The ear results cover every fixed interior peak on every edge, including cut-crossing peaks. The corner derivative is strictly negative per removed area. We now supply the missing uniform error control and the exact endpoint geometry.

Translate y to zero. Denote the vertices of a nearby strict-incidence triangle T by A,B,C, with old area k. For the edge AB, every actual one-point ear has the representation

    Q=(1+eta)[(1-theta)A+theta B]-eta C,
    eta>0, 0<theta<1.                                  (1)

Its added area is eta k, and its diagonal CQ crosses AB at Q0=(1-theta)A+theta B. Conversely (1) gives a convex quadrilateral conv(A,Q,B,C), since those diagonals cross in their relative interiors. Its old triangle and hence the source are retained.

## 2. A uniform expansion for peaks away from vertices

For a cut isolating A, write its old values at A,B,C as p,-q,-r, all positive in absolute value. The new tip value is

    z_eta=(1+eta)[p-(p+q)theta]+eta r.

The exact added cap and section data are

    Delta Q=eta k F(p,q,z_eta),
    Delta sigma=eta k G(p,q,z_eta),                     (2)

where

    F(p,q,z)=1-q^2/[(p+q)(q+z)]       if z>=0,
              p^2/[(p+q)(p-z)]       if z<=0;
    G(p,q,z)=2q/[(p+q)(q+z)]         if z>=0,
              2p/[(p+q)(p-z)]        if z<=0.           (3)

These are the exact area and coarea formulas for the ear triangle ABQ. The two branches agree at z=0. The other endpoint cut has the same formulas with its own positive and negative heights. The cut isolating C has no added cap or section: its values at both edge endpoints are negative, and (1) moves its tip value farther negative.

Restrict T to a sufficiently small closed coordinate neighborhood of T0. All its p,q,r lie in a fixed interval [m,N] with m>0; areas, cap areas and sections also have positive lower bounds. In (3), each relevant denominator is bounded below by m times 2m. The functions F and G are uniformly bounded and Lipschitz in z on the bounded tip range, including z=0. This follows either directly from their bounded one-sided derivatives and equality at zero, or by splitting an interval at zero. Their dependence on the positive p,q is likewise uniformly Lipschitz. Since z_eta-z_0=O(eta) uniformly, (2) gives a uniform O(eta^2) error for the full data vector (k,Q1,Q2,Q3,sigma1,sigma2,sigma3).

The function Phi_i of this data vector has bounded first and second derivatives on a slightly larger positive compact data set. Taylor's formula therefore gives

    Phi_i(conv(T,Q))=Phi_i(T)+eta D_i(T,theta)+O(eta^2), (4)

with one common remainder constant for all these T and theta in [0,1]. The coefficient D_i is continuous in T and theta because the matching branches F,G in (3) are continuous. This argument does not assume differentiability of G across a moving vertex transition.

Fix any delta in (0,1/2). The proved fixed-peak results give D_i(T0,theta)<0 on every edge for delta<=theta<=1-delta. Continuity on this compact set supplies a number c>0; shrinking the triangle neighborhood makes D_i(T,theta)<=-c there. The uniform remainder in (4) then gives, for one sufficiently small eta0>0,

    Phi_i(conv(T,Q))<Phi_i(T)<=2                       (5)

for all 0<eta<=eta0 and all those interior peaks. This is a justified use of compactness after proving a uniform remainder, not an inference from first derivatives alone.

## 3. Exact treatment of a peak approaching a vertex

Suppose theta is near zero, with eta small enough that

    b=(1+eta)theta<1.

Set

    a=eta/[1-(1+eta)theta],
    R=(1+a)A-aC,
    T_hat=conv(R,B,C).                                 (6)

Then Q=(1-b)R+bB, while A lies in the relative interior of RC. Consequently the quadrilateral in (1) is EXACTLY T_hat with the corner triangle conv(R,A,Q) removed. The retained and removed pieces share only the cut AQ. The removed area is

    E=k(a-eta)
      =k eta(1+eta)theta/[1-(1+eta)theta].              (7)

These identities follow by the barycentric coefficients in (1), and show every containment and intersection explicitly.

Choose a small ball about the old vertex A0 in which its own cut is positive and both other cuts are negative. Such a ball exists by strict incidence. First choose delta>0 sufficiently small that the initial edge portions of relative length at most delta lie in a smaller such ball, uniformly for nearby T. Then choose eta0 and the triangle neighborhood small enough that R,A,Q in (6) all belong to the first ball whenever theta<=delta and eta<=eta0. This is possible with a direct bound: for, say, delta<=1/4 and eta<=1/4, the denominator in (6) exceeds 1/2, so |R-A|<=2eta|A-C| and |Q-A|<=theta|B-A|+eta|Q0-C|. Edge lengths are uniformly bounded. No ratio eta/theta is restricted.

Thus the removed corner is wholly in one strict unique-signature sector and misses every source cutting line. All three sections of T_hat and the retained quadrilateral coincide; only the total area and that one cap lose E. The exact data change is therefore the one in the corner-removal theorem, even though AQ need not be parallel to the opposite facet. For a fixed T_hat, homothetically shrinking this corner about R supplies every smaller lost area, with the same cut-free property.

The corner-removal expression is a smooth function Psi(T_hat,E) of the nearby triangle data and E, with Psi(T_hat,0)=Phi_i(T_hat). Its E derivative is strictly negative at (T0,0) for removal at this vertex, by the proved corner theorem. The explicit positive cap/section denominators remain bounded away from zero. Hence there is a single neighborhood and a single E0>0 on which this derivative remains strictly negative. Formula (7) makes E uniformly small when eta is small. Therefore

    Phi_i(conv(T,Q))=Psi(T_hat,E)<Phi_i(T_hat)<=2.       (8)

The last inequality is the actual-triangle theorem, since T_hat stays near T0 and retains strict incidence and source interior. The argument at theta near one is identical with A and B exchanged. It handles theta tending to zero or one arbitrarily fast, including eta comparable to theta. The first-order ear coefficient may vanish in that limit; (8) does not divide by it.

Taking the minimum of finitely many admissible sizes for the three edges and their endpoints, and combining (5) and (8), proves a uniform one-ear statement for all nearby triangles, all theta in (0,1), and all sufficiently small positive eta.

## 4. Why every sufficiently close quadrilateral is covered

Let lambda_1,lambda_2,lambda_3 be the fixed barycentric coordinate functions of T0, and let L0 be the largest norm of their linear parts. If the Hausdorff distance from a quadrilateral K to T0 is epsilon, choose a vertex V_i of K maximizing lambda_i. Then lambda_i(V_i)>=1-L0 epsilon. Choose Z_i in T0 with |V_i-Z_i|<=epsilon. It follows that lambda_i(Z_i)>=1-2L0 epsilon and hence

    |V_i-P_i|<=epsilon+2L0 epsilon diam(T0).             (9)

For sufficiently small epsilon these three maximizing vertices are distinct. Thus their triangle T is in the required coordinate neighborhood of T0 and contains the fixed source in its interior. If K has only these three vertices, the triangle theorem applies directly. Otherwise its fourth vertex Q lies outside exactly one edge of T: the diagonals of a strict convex quadrilateral cross in their relative interiors. Its barycentric coordinates relative to T have one negative and two positive entries, giving exactly (1).

It remains to control eta=|K|/|T|-1 uniformly. Choose r>0 with r times the unit disk contained in T0. Bound (9) implies h_T>=h_T0-Cepsilon, where C=1+2L0 diam(T0). Thus, for small epsilon,

    (1-Cepsilon/r)T0 subset T,
    K subset (1+epsilon/r)T0.

Both inclusions follow by support functions and the fact h_T0>=r on unit normals. Consequently

    0<eta <= [(1+epsilon/r)/(1-Cepsilon/r)]^2-1,

which tends to zero uniformly. This puts K in the one-ear regime proved above and establishes the theorem.

The same homothetic inclusions imply continuity of cap areas and of the three through-source sections, since dilations about the source preserve the cuts and section rays. They justify preserving any initially strict rows. For every initially tight row, apply the proved neighborhood theorem and take the finite intersection.

## 5. Remaining scope

The construction proves an actual finite Hausdorff neighborhood among triangles and quadrilaterals. It is not a neighborhood theorem for arbitrary polygons or smooth bodies. A many-vertex perturbation can have simultaneous curved additions on several edges; reducing these to one ear while preserving all cap and section data is a separate problem. No such reduction is supplied here.
